**Original form.** Inspection scenarios prescribe systematic searches for particular fault classes.

**Claim supported.** Fault-specific scenario reading outperformed checklist/ad hoc under study conditions; meetings did not add net detection benefit

**Role.** DIRECT_INSPECTION_METHOD_EVIDENCE and within-program replication; source-defined detection outcome and bounded transfer

**Unsupported promotion.** 48 graduate students, two small event-driven SRSs and constrained crossover; not all industrial reviews or negotiation; naturally occurring faults rather than deliberately seeded faults

**Source id.** ERE-S-S027

**Locator.** §§3.4, 5.1–5.4, 6

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No claim of absolute first invention. Inspection scenario means a fault-focused reading procedure, not a behavioral use case or BDD example.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Where known fault classes and a suitable specification exist, use concrete reading procedures targeted at those faults, with locally validated cost and detection value.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_EMPIRICAL_METHOD

**Bearer or subject.** A requirements review and specified fault classes

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Ad hoc reading or generic checklist completion may not direct attention to the defects a reviewer must find.

**Mechanism.** Assign a reading procedure that guides the reviewer through representations/checks relevant to a fault, rather than merely naming a general quality.

**Mature or evolved form.** Retain targeted search with conditional comparisons and exploratory inquiry; distinguish a local useful finding, a comparative detection effect and net workflow benefit, and label qualitative practical cost justification as such.

**Expected payoff.** Higher detection of the targeted faults under the studied conditions.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** S026 reports better targeted-fault detection for scenario procedures in two study runs with 48 graduate students and two event-driven SRSs. This supports the stated comparative detection outcome, not an automatic total net benefit for every review workflow. The local-usefulness and cost judgments are separately scoped.

**Decision or consumer.** Review organizer choosing an inspection technique for a known risk.

**Alternative mechanisms.** Focused informal review or automated structural check when it discriminates the fault more cheaply.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Material known defect classes warrant inspection and can be operationalized as concrete reviewer tasks.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** An obvious low-impact textual correction does not need a team inspection.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Reviewers have appropriate domain/task competence; known faults represent relevant risks; technique costs are counted.

**Environment and boundary.** Inspection scenario means a fault-focused reading procedure, not a behavioral use case or BDD example.

**Scope and exclusions.** Inspection scenario means a fault-focused reading procedure, not a behavioral use case or BDD example. Excludes any target repository finding or inter-lineage ownership assignment.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Fault discovery informs a decision but does not itself settle stakeholder preference or authority.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Specification/version, risk/fault taxonomy, reading procedure, reviewer background, findings and adjudication.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Related property ids.** ERE-C0119; ERE-C0113

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-S10

**Limit.** Relations are conditional; see internal_relations, not all listed items are mandatory prerequisites

**Failure of assumptions.** Reviewers tick “consistent” without applying any check, then cite the experiment as evidence their unrelated checklist must improve quality.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Preparation, training and false-positive adjudication; increasing detection may not justify every extra review stage.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Retire a procedure when its fault class or artifact form no longer applies; reenter if incidents or changed artifacts reveal recurrence.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-S14

**Strongest objection.** The strongest original experiment uses students and constrained documents; procedural guidance can miss unanticipated defects.

**Known failures and misuses.** Reviewers tick “consistent” without applying any check, then cite the experiment as evidence their unrelated checklist must improve quality.

**Response or descendant form.** Treat comparative results as conditional, retain exploratory inquiry and test local usefulness.

**What changed and what did not.** Strengthens vague inspection advice into specified fault-search procedures while limiting empirical transfer.

**Residual limits.** Unknown faults, domain misunderstandings and representational blind spots remain.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** An inspection meeting or completed checklist is not equivalent to conducting a targeted search.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-S10

**Retention status.** CONTEXT_DEPENDENT

**Retention rationale.** Retain the bounded mechanism with explicit guard, evidence and cheap path. Treat comparative results as conditional, retain exploratory inquiry and test local usefulness.

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** Candidate challenged in Porter–Votta–Basili1995

**Original terminology.** Inspection meetings traditionally collect and discuss individual findings.

**Original form.** Inspection meetings traditionally collect and discuss individual findings.

**Original problem.** Repeated review ceremonies are justified by assumed inevitable quality gain.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-S08

**Influence or relation class.** ANALYTICAL_QUALIFICATION_OF_DOCUMENTED_BRANCH; see genealogy edges for evidence-backed historical relations

**Historical evidence and locators.** **Source id.** ERE-S-S026

**Locator.** §§II, IV–V

**Source id.** ERE-S-S017

**Locator.** pp. 22–24, 29–31; inquiry cycle and level-of-effort discussion

**Role.** ADJACENT_CONCEPTUAL_INQUIRY_MECHANISM distinguishing interpretation from collection; no meeting-effect comparison

**Unsupported promotion.** Meeting-scheduler exercise and rough effort extrapolation, not controlled industrial payoff; downstream rationale use not studied

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No claim of absolute first invention. Collection/detection function only; negotiation, learning, shared interpretation and authority decisions may independently justify a meeting.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Candidate universal claim: adding a collection meeting after individual review necessarily increases net relevant defect detection enough to justify the burden.

**Claim class.** NEGATIVE_CANDIDATE_PROCESS_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** An additional review meeting and its incremental effect

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Repeated review ceremonies are justified by assumed inevitable quality gain.

**Mechanism.** The rejected inference treats attendance/repetition as detection evidence without distinguishing new findings, lost findings and decisions.

**Mature or evolved form.** Separate functions and retain only the unresolved function and observed/context-supported value.

**Expected payoff.** Would guarantee quality from one more meeting; observed study does not support that.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** In the1995 study, meeting gains did not provide a net improvement over individual discovery; this is a bounded counterexample to necessity, not proof that meetings never help.

**Decision or consumer.** Review organizer deciding whether another meeting is necessary.

**Alternative mechanisms.** Asynchronous reconciliation of already known findings or a meeting aimed at a specific unresolved interpretation.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** An extra collection meeting is proposed solely because it is presumed to add defects.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** If evidence and dispositions already settle the decision, complete the decision without another detection ceremony.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Necessity would require positive net detection in every applicable situation, a claim defeated by a bounded counterexample.

**Environment and boundary.** Collection/detection function only; negotiation, learning, shared interpretation and authority decisions may independently justify a meeting.

**Scope and exclusions.** Collection/detection function only; negotiation, learning, shared interpretation and authority decisions may independently justify a meeting. Excludes any target repository finding or inter-lineage ownership assignment.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** A meeting can be needed to exercise a real decision right; that is separate from guaranteed defect-detection gain.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Individual findings before meeting, new findings, dismissed/lost findings, adjudication and time.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Related property ids.** ERE-C0114; ERE-C0113

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-S10

**Limit.** Relations are conditional; see internal_relations, not all listed items are mandatory prerequisites

**Failure of assumptions.** A collection meeting adds as many valid defects as it discards, with additional participant time; necessity of positive net detection is false.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Reviewer coordination and preparation plus potential suppression of valid individual findings.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Reject necessity; retain a meeting if its named information or decision function remains unresolved.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-S15

**Strongest objection.** Calling meetings waste from one experiment would overgeneralize just as much as requiring them universally.

**Known failures and misuses.** A collection meeting adds as many valid defects as it discards, with additional participant time; necessity of positive net detection is false.

**Response or descendant form.** Separate functions and retain only the unresolved function and observed/context-supported value.

**What changed and what did not.** Reject mandatory detection ceremony; preserve purposeful collective decisions.

**Residual limits.** Some benefits are difficult to quantify and require an explicit qualitative rationale.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** Repetition is not additional evidence.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-S10

**Retention status.** REJECTED_OR_DISFAVOURED

**Retention rationale.** Retain the rejection in the denominator, not an adoption candidate. Separate functions and retain only the unresolved function and observed/context-supported value.

A sufficiency challenge tests an asserted implication or universal process benefit; ordinary operational assessment evaluates the bounded source-informed rule. Mechanical record checks do not settle semantic, empirical or authority judgments.

**Domain.** integer

**Constraint.** Adjudication basis explicit

**Domain.** enum plus rationale

No quantification over all possible stakeholders, worlds or future changes. A universal sufficiency claim is refuted by a valid applicable counterexample; case PASS is not universal proof.

**Temporal and modal semantics.** Assessed at the named evidence/configuration snapshot. Hypothesized, desired, agreed and observed states remain distinct. Later changes require the stated invalidation procedure.

Mechanical schema checks can establish presence/identity, not domain truth or authority.

**Decidability and approximation.** Finite record checks are mechanically decidable. Semantic correspondence, legitimate representation, proxy validity and causal transfer generally require contextual judgment and may remain UNKNOWN. No claim of general decidability.

**Positive witness.** **Class.** ANALYTICAL_CONSTRUCTION_UNLESS_SOURCE_EXPLICITLY_IDENTIFIED

**Text.** A meeting addresses an unresolved contradictory interpretation and finds a new release-critical defect; its value is shown locally.

**Counterexample or failure witness.** **Class.** ANALYTICAL_CONSTRUCTION

**Text.** A collection meeting adds as many valid defects as it discards, with additional participant time; necessity of positive net detection is false.

**Unknown conditions.** The guard plausibly applies but required source, semantic interpretation, authority, context or observation is missing/disputed; insufficient evidence is not silently coded FAIL or PASS.

**Inapplicability conditions.** A duly authorized stakeholder negotiation is needed to choose between incompatible interests, regardless of defect count.

**False positive and false negative risks.** **False positive.** Repetition is not additional evidence.

**False negative.** Rejecting a legitimate cheap path, demanding irrelevant evidence, or treating an unrecorded but unresolved dimension as known false.

**Vacuity or proxy gaming risks.** An empty declared scope cannot pass merely because no obligations were listed: explain why the guard is inapplicable or why the scope is adequate. Repetition is not additional evidence.

**Change invalidation rule.** Change in meeting purpose, participant knowledge or unresolved questions changes applicability.

**Cost and cheaper alternative.** Reviewer coordination and preparation plus potential suppression of valid individual findings. Alternative: If evidence and dispositions already settle the decision, complete the decision without another detection ceremony.

**Evidence ceiling.** In the1995 study, meeting gains did not provide a net improvement over individual discovery; this is a bounded counterexample to necessity, not proof that meetings never help. The operational rule is a proposed audit discriminator, not a measured process-effect claim.

**Formalisation provenance.** Analytical operational reconstruction from inspected primary sources; no claim of a source-native theorem or universal algorithm.

**Operational evaluation.** **Rule.** For the detection-only necessity claim, nonpositive net relevant findings with positive cost is a FAIL counterexample. Positive net findings supports only that meeting/context. Missing before/after records yields UNKNOWN; meetings justified by another function are INAPPLICABLE to this detection claim.

**Fail.** An applicable observed contradiction, failed criterion or valid counterexample defeats the specified claim

**Unknown.** Relevant evidence/meaning/authority is missing, disputed or not discriminating

**Inapplicable.** An explicit guard excludes the claim; cheap path must be justified

**Empty scope rule.** Empty obligation/source sets never establish completeness by vacuity; show scope adequacy or label inapplicable/unknown.

**Currentness and invalidation.** Change in meeting purpose, participant knowledge or unresolved questions changes applicability.

### Evidence limits and open questions

**Unknown conditions.** The guard plausibly applies but required source, semantic interpretation, authority, context or observation is missing/disputed; insufficient evidence is not silently coded FAIL or PASS.

**Inapplicability conditions.** A requirement contains an explicit impossible numeric condition; direct domain reasoning resolves it without quality-score research.

**False positive and false negative risks.** **False positive.** A sophisticated statistical model cannot repair an invalid construct or irrelevant task.

**False negative.** Rejecting a legitimate cheap path, demanding irrelevant evidence, or treating an unrecorded but unresolved dimension as known false.

**Vacuity or proxy gaming risks.** An empty declared scope cannot pass merely because no obligations were listed: explain why the guard is inapplicable or why the scope is adequate. A sophisticated statistical model cannot repair an invalid construct or irrelevant task.

**Change invalidation rule.** Changed task, reader competence, domain, wording feature or outcome definition invalidates broad transfer.

**Cost and cheaper alternative.** Studies and measurement can exceed local benefit; reuse relevant bounded evidence before collecting new data. Alternative: A clear direct contradiction can be corrected without an experimental quality model.

**Evidence ceiling.** 25-participant four-statement domain-modeling experiment finds different effects for passive voice and ambiguous pronouns, with important transfer and measurement limits. The operational rule is a proposed audit discriminator, not a measured process-effect claim.

**Formalisation provenance.** Analytical operational reconstruction from inspected primary sources; no claim of a source-native theorem or universal algorithm.

**Operational evaluation.** **Rule.** A claimed quality benefit must name the affected activity and outcome, describe a causal/operational path and have evidence appropriate to that context. Direct contradictory task evidence FAILS the claimed benefit; mere conformity with no outcome warrant is UNKNOWN. Pure normative compliance is evaluated separately.

**Outcomes.** **Pass.** Required evidence supports the bounded claim within scope; no universal extrapolation

**Fail.** An applicable observed contradiction, failed criterion or valid counterexample defeats the specified claim

**Unknown.** Relevant evidence/meaning/authority is missing, disputed or not discriminating

**Inapplicable.** An explicit guard excludes the claim; cheap path must be justified

**Empty scope rule.** Empty obligation/source sets never establish completeness by vacuity; show scope adequacy or label inapplicable/unknown.

**Positive witness or worked example.** Ambiguous pronoun removal changes readers’ domain-model associations under a declared task; evidence supports attention to that ambiguity in similar work.

**Negative witness or counterexample.** A tool penalizes all passive voice equally and asserts equivalent downstream harm for each occurrence despite little relevant effect in the task evidence.

**Non trigger example.** A requirement contains an explicit impossible numeric condition; direct domain reasoning resolves it without quality-score research.

**Observability and missingness.** Task outputs/errors, duration, participant/context descriptors and treatment comparison. Missing evidence remains UNKNOWN unless an explicit contradicted claim is being tested.

**Currentness and invalidation.** Changed task, reader competence, domain, wording feature or outcome definition invalidates broad transfer.

### Evidence limits and open questions

**Evidence ceiling.** 25-participant four-statement domain-modeling experiment finds different effects for passive voice and ambiguous pronouns, with important transfer and measurement limits. Source access levels bind every claim; schema completeness is not domain validation.

**Transferability limits.** A particular wording defect can harm one task yet be harmless or useful elsewhere; study measures not all requirement validity. Sparse task-specific evidence, unmeasured interactions and imperfect context variables remain.

**Unverified or open questions.** A context-matched replication or actual-consumer task observation that can reverse the rule priority.

**Next discriminator.** A context-matched replication or actual-consumer task observation that can reverse the rule priority.

**Affected finding ids.** ERE-RF-F02; ERE-RF-F03

**Disposition reference.** EVOLVED_REQUIREMENTS_ENGINEERING_VALIDATION_REPORT.md, findings/corrections section

**Original problem.** A completed task list can conceal loss of the problem, cross-team constraints and decision ownership.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A revised requirement remains justified only when the changed claim, its authority, its supporting feedback, and the impact on dependent commitments are recoverable for the decision that consumes it.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A versioned requirement/change decision, not the backlog as a whole.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A completed task list can conceal loss of the problem, cross-team constraints and decision ownership.

**Mechanism.** Separate evidence of a newly learned need from authorization to change a commitment; preserve stable constraints and connect discovery to delivery through explicit decisions.

**Mature or evolved form.** Lightweight revision records attached to the actual change, with risk-proportionate impact analysis; discovery and delivery can overlap without becoming isolated handoffs.

**Expected payoff.** Makes change responsive while keeping accountability and test correspondence inspectable.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** N004/N005/N043 provide field observations and practitioner judgments; they do not establish a universal reduction in rework or an optimal documentation volume.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A versioned requirement/change decision, not the backlog as a whole.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a reversible wording clarification with no changed interpretation or dependent artifact, keep the old/new wording and a short reason in the existing issue; no separate committee or dual-track organization is required.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A requirement, acceptance criterion, data assumption or externally committed scope changes during iterative delivery.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a reversible wording clarification with no changed interpretation or dependent artifact, keep the old/new wording and a short reason in the existing issue; no separate committee or dual-track organization is required.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** A decision owner can be identified; affected constraints are at least partially known; feedback is not automatically representative of every stakeholder.

**Environment and boundary.** Applies to the requirement revision, whether agile, plan-driven or hybrid; does not demand all discovery happen before implementation.

**Scope and exclusions.** Applies to the requirement revision, whether agile, plan-driven or hybrid; does not demand all discovery happen before implementation. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: A fresh backlog proves requirements validity; all change is good; dual-track is universally superior.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Local stakeholder/contract/policy authority must be established separately; Agile principles themselves confer no power to waive a contract.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Old/new text, feedback origin and sampling context, named decision authority, date, affected goals/tests/interfaces and unresolved disagreements.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0204; ERE-C0211; ERE-C0212

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N01; ERE-T-N02

**Failure of assumptions.** Unavailable stakeholders or hidden dependencies may make the change provisional; the record must carry that uncertainty rather than treating owner assignment as validation.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Impact analysis and keeping links alive consume time; use scope/risk to select the links and evidence worth maintaining.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Close when the revised commitment is retired and downstream artifacts cannot rely on it; reopen after new conflicting feedback or changed authority.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N01

**Strongest objection.** Formal change control can prevent useful learning and become a second backlog whose maintenance costs exceed its decision value.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: a delivery team removes a slow response criterion after tests fail and marks the original goal done without asking the owner. Game by classifying every semantic change as editorial or excluding inconvenient dependent commitments.

**Response or descendant form.** Retain change authority and evidence continuity, strip mandatory meetings/documents; scale investigation to consequence and uncertainty.

**What changed and what did not.** Change responsiveness is preserved; record form, role names and sprint ceremonies are contingent.

**Residual limits.** No record can manufacture unavailable stakeholder judgment or complete impact knowledge.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** Backlog grooming frequency and number of approval fields are proxies, not the mechanism.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N01; ERE-T-N02

**Retention status.** RETAINED_IN_EVOLVED_FORM

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Retain change authority and evidence continuity, strip mandatory meetings/documents; scale investigation to consequence and uncertainty.

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** RELAX2009/2010 distinguishes requirements that tolerate uncertainty from critical invariants; later runtime work changes checking properties as well as implementations.

**Original terminology.** RELAX-ed requirements; invariants; ENV/MON/REL/DEP

**Original form.** Source-specific formulation recorded in the linked original works; this record separates the reusable mechanism from named method/notation.

**Original problem.** A system can appear adaptive by weakening its target until any behavior counts as success.

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No claim of first invention outside the inspected sources. RELAX2009/2010 distinguishes requirements that tolerate uncertainty from critical invariants; later runtime work changes checking properties as well as implementations.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Relaxing a requirement is justified only inside a previously authorized envelope, with preserved critical constraints and an explicit record of which target was used.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A runtime selection of an admissible requirement interpretation/target.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A system can appear adaptive by weakening its target until any behavior counts as success.

**Mechanism.** Specify what may vary, under which observed uncertainty, and what must not vary; compare candidate adaptations against that boundary.

**Mature or evolved form.** Separate implementation adaptation, permitted requirement relaxation and true renegotiation; monitor each using its declared version.

**Expected payoff.** Makes tolerable degradation explicit while exposing unauthorized goal substitution.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** RELAX provides formal language and cases, not independent industrial efficacy; later observer work demonstrates a different, narrower technical problem.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A runtime selection of an admissible requirement interpretation/target.

**Non trigger example.** A help-page typo with no control or safety-information effect can use a brief impact decision.

**Observability and missingness.** Domain state, issued/omitted action, timing and feedback observed separately from controller’s internal belief. Hazard context, responsible controller or feedback latency cannot be established.

**Currentness and invalidation.** Changed control structure, sensor/actuator semantics, environment, hazard or responsibility.

### Evidence limits and open questions

**Evidence ceiling.** **Strongest supported claim.** N020 is a method handbook with worked examples; N042 illustrates that specified interfaces can fail in implementation/coordination; N028 warns that monitors themselves have costs. No universal comparative accident reduction inferred.

**Stronger unsupported claims.** All four control-action categories were filled, therefore every hazard is controlled.

**Transferability limits.** Identified hazards/control interactions within an operating envelope; no complete safety case or certification claimed. Coverage of rare/unimagined interactions and quantified field benefit remain unsupported here.

**Unverified or open questions.** Hazard context, responsible controller or feedback latency cannot be established. Coverage of rare/unimagined interactions and quantified field benefit remain unsupported here.

**Next discriminator.** Adversarial scenario review and evidence that actual control/feedback behavior matches each hazardous context.

**Original terminology.** Security goals; operational constraints; PO.1.2

### Claim and mechanism

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A scoped security requirement and its threat/policy rationale.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A security checklist can be complete as paperwork yet disconnected from assets, actors and the threat that motivates a control.

**Mechanism.** Derive candidate constraints from goals and risk scenarios; prioritize and inspect their fit, then revise when threat, architecture or policy changes.

**Mature or evolved form.** Risk-tailored elicitation with explicit exception decisions and feedback; no universal nine-step ceremony or fixed control list.

**Expected payoff.** Separates a justified protection need from solution fashion and exposes gaps or trade-offs.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A scoped security requirement and its threat/policy rationale.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Assets, services or trust boundaries face relevant adversarial misuse or a security obligation applies.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a minor change wholly within a validated protection boundary, check the affected scenario/control and version; do not reconstruct the entire threat model.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Threat model and business impact are credible; feasible controls and test conditions can be specified.

**Environment and boundary.** Specified assets, trust boundaries and attack conditions; not a claim of absence of all vulnerabilities.

**Scope and exclusions.** Specified assets, trust boundaries and attack conditions; not a claim of absence of all vulnerabilities. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: SSDF conformance guarantees secure software; SQUARE universally reduces cost by a fixed multiplier.

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N04; ERE-T-N05

**Failure of assumptions.** Changed attacker capability or overlooked trust boundary invalidates apparent protection; acceptance of residual risk must be explicit.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Threat modeling and review effort; checklist overload can reduce attention as SQUARE’s negative findings show.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** After asset/threat path ends; re-enter on new vulnerability, boundary, policy, supplier or adversary capability.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N06

**Strongest objection.** Risk estimates can be speculative and prioritization can rationalize underprotection; inspection may consume time without finding defects.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: require encryption everywhere while leaving the trusted export role able to disclose the same data improperly. Treat the presence of a risk register or the word secure as the protection requirement.

**Response or descendant form.** Use explicit scenarios and residual-risk decisions; preserve the original case failures rather than declaring every SQUARE step empirically proven.

**What changed and what did not.** Threat rationale remains necessary; particular workshops, scoring methods and control products are optional.

**Residual limits.** No general breach-reduction or cost-multiplier evidence established.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** Nine completed steps and a signed checklist do not demonstrate effective security.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N04; ERE-T-N05

**Retention status.** DOMAIN_SPECIFIC

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Use explicit scenarios and residual-risk decisions; preserve the original case failures rather than declaring every SQUARE step empirically proven.

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** LINDDUN2010/2011 explicitly translates STRIDE-compatible data-flow modeling into privacy threat analysis; its discussion identifies relational threats beyond local disclosure.

**Original terminology.** Linkability; identifiability; non-repudiation; detectability; disclosure; unawareness; noncompliance

**Source id.** ERE-S-N019

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No claim of first invention outside the inspected sources. LINDDUN2010/2011 explicitly translates STRIDE-compatible data-flow modeling into privacy threat analysis; its discussion identifies relational threats beyond local disclosure.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A privacy requirement must identify the people/data relationships and uses it constrains, including linkage or inferred information where material; a security control alone is insufficient evidence.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A data relationship/use constraint across flows, stores, actors and time.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Confidentiality can hold while lawful-looking collection, linkage, inference or retention undermines privacy.

**Mechanism.** Model privacy-relevant assets and relationships, elicit threat paths, then derive scoped constraints or mitigations while preserving conflicts with accountability and utility.

**Mature or evolved form.** Combine lightweight GO discovery or deeper DFD-based analysis with purpose/context and temporal inference review; do not equate a taxonomy pass with legal compliance.

**Expected payoff.** Surfaces privacy harms that access-control-only requirements can miss.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** N018 establishes the method/representation argument and limitations; N019 documents available lower-cost methods. No comprehensive legal assurance or comparative field outcome established.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A data relationship/use constraint across flows, stores, actors and time.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a genuinely nonpersonal static asset, record the basis for that scope; for a small personal-data feature, use a short relationship/use sketch and GO-style prompts before adopting a full model.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Personal or inferentially identifying data is collected, linked, inferred, retained, disclosed or used in a potentially harmful context.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a genuinely nonpersonal static asset, record the basis for that scope; for a small personal-data feature, use a short relationship/use sketch and GO-style prompts before adopting a full model.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Important identities, relationships, recipients and inference possibilities are represented; social/legal context is reviewed by appropriate owners.

**Environment and boundary.** Privacy threat analysis within stated data and actors; not a complete interpretation of all privacy law.

**Scope and exclusions.** Privacy threat analysis within stated data and actors; not a complete interpretation of all privacy law. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: Encrypted data is private; LINDDUN proves compliance with all privacy law.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Stakeholder privacy goals and applicable obligations require their own authority record; LINDDUN is a method.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Data items/subjects, sources, flows, purposes, recipients, retention and inference/linkage assumptions with justified mitigation.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0204; ERE-C0206; ERE-C0209; ERE-C0211

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Failure of assumptions.** A DFD that omits cross-flow correlations or inferred information can pass local checks and still miss the privacy problem.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Keeping data maps/current purposes aligned; detailed modeling is costly and may expose sensitive information itself.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** When processing/retention ends and evidence supports removal; re-enter on new linkage, recipient, purpose or inference capability.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N07

**Strongest objection.** Taxonomies can overfit technical assets and underrepresent lived privacy, power and inferred knowledge.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: encrypted datasets share a stable identifier, enabling a recipient to reconstruct a sensitive profile despite confidential transport. Call data anonymous merely because names were removed; accept every threat as policy-compliant without inspecting policy.

**Response or descendant form.** Keep relationship and context annotations, affected-person perspectives and unresolved inference risks; combine privacy and security without collapsing them.

**What changed and what did not.** Data-flow reuse remains efficient; confidentiality and privacy remain distinct claims.

**Residual limits.** Method coverage and whole-jurisdiction legal completeness are unsupported.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A privacy impact form or seven-category check is not evidence that relationships and uses are appropriate.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Retention status.** DOMAIN_SPECIFIC

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Keep relationship and context annotations, affected-person perspectives and unresolved inference risks; combine privacy and security without collapsing them.

## ERE-C0208 — Scoped whole-process accessibility conformance

### Identity

**Property id.** ERE-C0208

**Property name.** Scoped whole-process accessibility conformance

**Lineage id.** EVOLVED_REQUIREMENTS_ENGINEERING

**Property families.** ERE-FAM07; ERE-FAM16

**Record kind.** BOUNDED_PROPERTY

**Parent ids.** None recorded.

**Alias or supersession ids.** None recorded.

**Discovery source ids.** ERE-S-N021; ERE-S-N022

**Native family labels.** ACCESSIBILITY_REQUIREMENTS; CONFORMANCE_BOUNDARY

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** WCAG2.2 carries public testable success criteria and explicit conformance requirements; the2026 WCAG3 draft remains a different status.

**Original terminology.** Full pages; complete processes; accessibility-supported ways; non-interference

**Original form.** Source-specific formulation recorded in the linked original works; this record separates the reusable mechanism from named method/notation.

**Original problem.** Passing isolated component checks can hide an inaccessible step in the user’s complete task.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-N08

**Influence or relation class.** See typed genealogy_edges; shared purpose alone is not direct influence.

**Historical evidence and locators.** **Source id.** ERE-S-N021

**Locators.** Status; §5.2 conformance requirements

**Source id.** ERE-S-N022

**Locators.** Status of this document

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No claim of first invention outside the inspected sources. WCAG2.2 carries public testable success criteria and explicit conformance requirements; the2026 WCAG3 draft remains a different status.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A WCAG2.2 conformance claim must state level/version and cover the full pages and complete processes in its claimed scope, with required technology support and non-interference; it must not be expanded into universal accessibility.

**Claim class.** SCOPED_NORMATIVE_CONDITION

**Bearer or subject.** A scoped web-content/process conformance claim.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Passing isolated component checks can hide an inaccessible step in the user’s complete task.

**Mechanism.** Evaluate the selected normative criteria over the whole claimed pages/process, including dependencies and alternate paths required by the conformance rules.

**Mature or evolved form.** Combine criteria-based evaluation with user/task validation for needs beyond the standard; keep recommendation and draft statuses distinct.

**Expected payoff.** Prevents partial interface evidence from being advertised as complete-process conformance.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** N021 is the normative basis itself; it establishes what the conformance claim means, not that conformity meets every user need.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A scoped web-content/process conformance claim.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For an isolated prototype with no conformance claim, perform relevant keyboard/text/contrast checks and record limitations; no false complete-process certificate.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A product or requirement asserts WCAG2.2 conformance or uses it as an adopted acceptance criterion.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For an isolated prototype with no conformance claim, perform relevant keyboard/text/contrast checks and record limitations; no false complete-process certificate.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** The claimed process and supported technology configuration are identified; evaluators can inspect every applicable step.

**Environment and boundary.** Web content and scoped complete processes under WCAG2.2; other platforms, laws and individual needs require separate analysis.

**Scope and exclusions.** Web content and scoped complete processes under WCAG2.2; other platforms, laws and individual needs require separate analysis. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: WCAG2.2 conformance proves accessibility for everyone; WCAG3 is already the replacement standard.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** W3C normative Recommendation; binding force arises only from an independent adoption/legal basis. WCAG3 draft does not replace it.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Version/level, page/process inventory, technology/accessibility support, criterion results and unresolved steps.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0204; ERE-C0201; ERE-C0212

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N04; ERE-T-N06

**Failure of assumptions.** An untested or failing mandatory process step blocks the whole-process claim; inability to inspect yields unknown, not pass.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Manual and assistive-technology checks remain costly; automate only what the criterion and tool can actually assess.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** When content/process is removed; re-enter after flow, component, technology-support or criterion-version changes.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N08

**Strongest objection.** Compliance can become a checklist substitute for the actual experience of disabled users.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: accessible product pages lead to an inaccessible payment dialog, while the site advertises complete checkout conformance. Define the claimed process to exclude the only inaccessible step.

**Response or descendant form.** Honor the precise conformance boundary and separately validate user needs not covered by the standard.

**What changed and what did not.** Normative criteria remain useful; a conformance result has limited scope.

**Residual limits.** No universal user-need coverage or legal safe harbor follows.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A badge or high scanner score is not complete-process evidence.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N04; ERE-T-N06

**Retention status.** DOMAIN_SPECIFIC

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Honor the precise conformance boundary and separately validate user needs not covered by the standard.

**Predicate kind.** NORMATIVE_REQUIREMENT

**Cost and cheaper alternative.** Manual and assistive-technology checks remain costly; automate only what the criterion and tool can actually assess. For an isolated prototype with no conformance claim, perform relevant keyboard/text/contrast checks and record limitations; no false complete-process certificate.

**Evidence ceiling.** N021 is the normative basis itself; it establishes what the conformance claim means, not that conformity meets every user need. No universal user-need coverage or legal safe harbor follows.

### Genealogy

**Original terminology.** Sustainability design; direct, indirect and systemic effects; environmental/social/individual/economic/technical dimensions

**Original form.** Source-specific formulation recorded in the linked original works; this record separates the reusable mechanism from named method/notation.

**Original problem.** An energy metric or agreeable sustainability statement can conceal displaced harms, rebound effects or incompatible horizons.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-N09

**Influence or relation class.** See typed genealogy_edges; shared purpose alone is not direct influence.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A sustainability requirement is interpretable only with a declared effect, affected parties/system boundary, time horizon and evidence model; one metric cannot silently stand for all sustainability dimensions.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A scoped sustainability claim and the causal/measurement boundary used to judge it.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** An energy metric or agreeable sustainability statement can conceal displaced harms, rebound effects or incompatible horizons.

**Mechanism.** Identify relevant dimensions and effects, distinguish direct measurements from hypothesized systemic consequences, and surface trade-offs before selecting thresholds.

**Mature or evolved form.** Use a small number of decision-relevant measures plus qualitative impact arguments and explicit unknowns; do not force all dimensions into one unsupported scalar.

**Expected payoff.** Makes hidden trade-offs and evidence gaps visible to the decision owner.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** Manifesto is normative advocacy; interview/survey studies identify perceptions and adoption obstacles, not measured benefit from this proposed property.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A scoped sustainability claim and the causal/measurement boundary used to judge it.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a small local optimization, state its narrow energy/cost boundary and avoid a whole-sustainability claim; a short impact screen can decide whether deeper analysis is needed.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A requirement claims sustainability benefit or a choice materially affects long-lived environmental/social/economic/technical outcomes.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a small local optimization, state its narrow energy/cost boundary and avoid a whole-sustainability claim; a short impact screen can decide whether deeper analysis is needed.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Causal links and affected populations can be described; chosen horizon and trade-off authority are explicit.

**Environment and boundary.** Declared system, lifecycle and effects; no automatic assertion that every project needs five complete metric programs.

**Scope and exclusions.** Declared system, lifecycle and effects; no automatic assertion that every project needs five complete metric programs. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: Energy efficiency equals sustainability; practitioner agreement proves outcome improvement.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Stakeholder/mission values or adopted policy set priorities; manifesto advocacy does not supply binding thresholds.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Baseline, units, lifecycle boundary, population, horizon, measured versus modeled effects, allocation assumptions and decision rationale.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0204; ERE-C0207; ERE-C0210

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Failure of assumptions.** Benefits can reverse when workload, energy mix, retention, hardware lifecycle or behavior changes; record the conditional claim.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Lifecycle/systemic modeling can be expensive and uncertain; prioritize effects likely to change the decision.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** When the decision/effect path ends; re-enter after workload, boundary, horizon or stakeholder-priority changes.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N09

**Strongest objection.** Broad sustainability language can be too vague to guide engineering, while narrow metrics are easier to optimize.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: report lower joules per request as a net environmental gain despite a large increase in total requests and ignored hardware turnover. Use sustainable as an unmeasurable adjective or combine incompatible dimensions with arbitrary weights.

**Response or descendant form.** Keep narrow metrics useful but name their scope; use explicit qualitative judgment for broader effects rather than pretend one score settles them.

**What changed and what did not.** Multidimensional concern remains; any particular taxonomy, workshop or weighting scheme is contingent.

**Residual limits.** No general evidence found that a particular RE sustainability method improves net sustainability; this is a bounded search conclusion, not absence across the field.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A sustainability workshop or carbon label is not evidence of the claimed lifecycle outcome.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Retention status.** ASSUMPTION_SENSITIVE

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Keep narrow metrics useful but name their scope; use explicit qualitative judgment for broader effects rather than pretend one score settles them.

### Claim and mechanism

**Bearer or subject.** A statistical performance claim about a specific configured system on a defined population and operating envelope.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A high aggregate test score can be treated as deterministic safety, fairness or useful performance in a different population.

**Mechanism.** Choose decision-relevant error types/subgroups and stress conditions; evaluate independent evidence with uncertainty and preserve distinctions among accuracy, safety, fairness and utility.

**Mature or evolved form.** Conditional acceptance plus operational monitoring and requalification; rare or unobserved conditions remain unsupported instead of inheriting the aggregate score.

**Expected payoff.** Prevents overgeneralization and makes acceptance disagreements inspectable.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A statistical performance claim about a specific configured system on a defined population and operating envelope.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a deterministic component with a finite exact contract and no sampling inference, use direct correctness tests; a statistical performance dossier is unnecessary.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Behavior or acceptance depends on learned models, stochastic outputs or data distributions.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a deterministic component with a finite exact contract and no sampling inference, use direct correctness tests; a statistical performance dossier is unnecessary.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Evaluation sampling, labels and loss definitions fit the intended decision; dependence/leakage and subgroup coverage are considered.

**Environment and boundary.** The declared population/envelope and configuration; does not guarantee all future behavior or collapse distinct harms into one score.

**Scope and exclusions.** The declared population/envelope and configuration; does not guarantee all future behavior or collapse distinct harms into one score. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: Benchmark accuracy proves safety/fairness; a confidence interval covers unknown distribution shift.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Population/envelope definition, collection/labeling version, model/prompt/tool versions, holdout provenance, metric/loss, threshold rationale and uncertainty method.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A model card or benchmark leaderboard rank is not the statistical acceptance argument.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Machine checking of a requirement supports the intended claim only when input evidence, candidate interpretations, representation semantics and domain validation are connected; unresolved ambiguity must remain explicit.

**Claim class.** BOUNDED_ENGINEERING_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** A natural-language/domain-claim to machine representation correspondence.

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A syntactically valid formula can encode a wrong actor, exception, quantifier or temporal interpretation.

**Mechanism.** Expose interpretation choices and map source fragments/terms to representation; validate distinguishing positive and negative behaviors with a domain-capable reviewer before treating formula results as requirement results.

**Mature or evolved form.** Use controlled text, small executable checks or formal models according to the claim; preserve unknown interpretations and finite/infinite-trace semantics.

**Expected payoff.** Separates well-formedness and formal satisfiability from stakeholder meaning and catches plausible but wrong translations.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** N032 demonstrates tool semantics; N033/N034 evaluate limited translation sets with explicit correction/oracle limits. N040 shows linguistic screening can complement review without proving absence of ambiguity. N044 strengthens the formal transformation lane: termination/well-formedness theorem and separate oracle-based semantic testing remain distinct from stakeholder validity.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A natural-language/domain-claim to machine representation correspondence.

**Alternative mechanisms.** A short qualitative requirement may be best reviewed through concrete examples and a structured statement; no AST, temporal logic or compiler is required.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A textual/domain requirement is extracted, formalized, checked or used to generate tests/decisions automatically.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** A short qualitative requirement may be best reviewed through concrete examples and a structured statement; no AST, temporal logic or compiler is required.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Input scope and vocabulary are stable; reviewer understands the domain; representation can express the intended alternatives.

**Environment and boundary.** The expressed claim under declared semantics; not unexpressed stakeholder needs or truth of all domain assumptions.

**Scope and exclusions.** The expressed claim under declared semantics; not unexpressed stakeholder needs or truth of all domain assumptions. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: Parseable means correct; model-checking proves stakeholder intent; generated tests independently validate generated requirements.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** The tool is an interpreter/proposer. Interpretation and acceptance require the appropriate domain/requirement authority.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Source version/spans, vocabulary and units, candidate parses, selected interpretation/rationale, representation and semantics version, review witnesses.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0201; ERE-C0202; ERE-C0210; ERE-C0215

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N07; ERE-T-N08

**Failure of assumptions.** If representation cannot express the intended property or reviewers cannot distinguish interpretations, keep ambiguity/unknown rather than force a parse.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Human review/correction, formal-language expertise and trace design; claimed tool savings must include this effort.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** After requirement/representation is retired; re-enter on text/context/vocabulary/semantics/tool/model changes.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N12

**Strongest objection.** Formalization may make a wrong interpretation look authoritative and impose more review effort than direct human reasoning.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed example: every request eventually gets an acknowledgment is mistranslated as some request gets one; formula is satisfiable and tests derived from it repeat the error. A formula true on all traces, unreachable trigger or trivial witness set can pass checks without conveying the requirement.

**Response or descendant form.** Separate lexical/syntactic/semantic/domain checks, keep source spans and use discriminating witnesses; choose a cheaper structured review when adequate.

**What changed and what did not.** Machine reasoning remains valuable about the chosen model; it cannot decide the intended social/domain meaning by itself.

**Residual limits.** No general complete NL-to-formal translation or autonomous domain-valid requirement generation established.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** An AST, formula, generated test suite or tool PASS is not semantic validation.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N07; ERE-T-N08

**Retention status.** RETAINED_IN_EVOLVED_FORM

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Separate lexical/syntactic/semantic/domain checks, keep source spans and use discriminating witnesses; choose a cheaper structured review when adequate.

**Decision or consumer.** The actor deciding whether the named claim may be accepted, changed, reused or relied upon: A comparative effectiveness claim for a specified human/tool workflow.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For occasional low-stakes drafting, compare a few representative tasks and manually review output; do not claim a general productivity effect from that pilot.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A tool/LLM is recommended or accepted because it allegedly saves time, improves correctness or replaces a human requirements activity.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For occasional low-stakes drafting, compare a few representative tasks and manually review output; do not claim a general productivity effect from that pilot.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Baseline is competent and comparable; outcome labels and loss trade-offs fit the actual task; evaluated users/models represent intended use.

**Environment and boundary.** Specified tasks, experience level, model/version, prompting/workflow and data; no automatic transfer to professional or safety-critical use.

**Scope and exclusions.** Specified tasks, experience level, model/version, prompting/workflow and data; no automatic transfer to professional or safety-critical use. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: ARTEMIS trace-count reduction is observed human-time savings; nl2spec interactive accuracy is autonomous accuracy; one negative novice study condemns every LLM.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Research evidence informs adoption; it does not grant a model requirement-approval authority.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Study date, sample selection/size, tasks, labels, baselines, models/snapshots, prompts/configuration, interaction/correction traces, costs and contamination assessment.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0210; ERE-C0212; ERE-C0214; ERE-C0215

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N07; ERE-T-N08

**Failure of assumptions.** Opaque training data, model drift, weak oracle or unmeasured review effort reduces the ceiling of the claimed effect.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Evaluation costs can be significant; use smaller consequential pilots before broad comparative studies, but state their limited inference.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Re-evaluate after model/workflow/user/task distribution change or evidence of deterioration.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N13

**Strongest objection.** Full workflow studies are expensive and benchmarks can still be useful for comparing technical mechanisms.

**Known failures and misuses.** Observed bounded example: a34-novice crossover finds no clear time benefit and a direction of lower inspection F1 with mixed GPT-4o/4.1 support; uncertainty and preprint status remain. Measure easy formatting while claiming domain-valid requirements; omit expensive correction cases from time totals.

**Response or descendant form.** Retain technical benchmarks with narrow labels; require broader evidence only for broader adoption/productivity claims.

**What changed and what did not.** Benchmarks remain informative; their claim scope must not expand silently.

**Residual limits.** Professional multi-organization longitudinal cost/quality evidence for current LLM requirements workflows remains a material gap.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A high F1, tool demo, released ZIP or human-in-the-loop label does not establish net benefit.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N07; ERE-T-N08

**Retention status.** STRONGLY_RETAINED

**Retention rationale.** Retained only for its named bearer/trigger with the listed evidence ceiling and cheaper alternative. Retain technical benchmarks with narrow labels; require broader evidence only for broader adoption/productivity claims.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** The metric’s unit, functional unit, scope and time period are defined; equivalence with wider effects requires separate evidence.

**Environment and boundary.** The supersession concerns completeness, not the usefulness of a properly scoped environmental requirement.

**Scope and exclusions.** The supersession concerns completeness, not the usefulness of a properly scoped environmental requirement. Excluded or unsupported stronger claims: Energy metrics are useless; one carbon number settles all sustainability dimensions; perceived concern proves net outcome improvement.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Stakeholder/domain decisions define acceptable effects and tradeoffs; the manifesto is advocacy, not binding law or an empirical effect guarantee.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Energy/carbon measurement boundary, time horizon, functional unit, measurement model, affected parties and omitted effects.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** **Property dependencies.** ERE-C0209

**Tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Failure of assumptions.** Indirect demand changes or social/economic consequences can make a locally favorable proxy inadequate for a broader claim.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Whole-system effects can be difficult to quantify; a narrower honest requirement can be cheaper than an unsupported universal score.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Keep C0223 as superseded history and use C0209 for the stronger structured form; revisit if scope/effects or measurement models change.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-N23

**Strongest objection.** A narrow measurable target can motivate useful action where wider analysis is expensive or uncertain.

**Known failures and misuses.** Constructed counterexample: energy per transaction falls while transaction volume increases enough to raise total energy; the local metric is advertised as complete sustainability. Choose the easiest boundary and omit the activities whose impacts rose.

**Response or descendant form.** Preserve the useful narrow target and explicitly bound its claim; C0209 supplies the stronger interpretable form.

**What changed and what did not.** Energy/carbon can matter materially; a single metric does not inherit all sustainability meanings.

**Residual limits.** Net sustainability outcomes are not established by the perception studies in this corpus.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** A carbon dashboard or green score without effect/boundary disclosure is a proxy.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-N05; ERE-T-N06

**Retention status.** SUPERSEDED_BY_STRONGER_FORM

**Retention rationale.** SUPERSEDED_BY_STRONGER_FORM C0209; retain useful narrow energy measures with explicit boundaries, and preserve this incomplete candidate in the population.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Prioritization can expose judgments and tradeoffs when the scale, contributors, exclusions and decision rights are inspectable; numerical consistency does not establish legitimate or accurate utility.

**Claim class.** QUALIFIED_METHOD_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** A versioned requirements-prioritization decision

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Hidden rankings, false precision and collapsing mandatory obligations into preferences.

**Mechanism.** Keep raw judgments and their stated scale, separate non-negotiable conditions, inspect disagreement and compare a cheaper ordering procedure.

**Mature or evolved form.** Retain inspectable judgments while making the scoring method conditional; compare ordinal and lightweight alternatives.

**Expected payoff.** Makes the basis of selection challengeable and revisable.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R001 demonstrates industrial use; R003 compares two procedures and shows tool/context dependence. Neither establishes universal business value.

**Decision or consumer.** People choosing the next scope or deciding whether elicitation effort is justified.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For two obvious, reversible choices, an explained ordinal ordering and an explicit mandatory list can suffice.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Several genuinely negotiable alternatives compete for scarce resources and someone needs to understand why one outranks another.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For two obvious, reversible choices, an explained ordinal ordering and an explicit mandatory list can suffice.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Participants understand the alternatives; scale semantics are stated; mandatory exclusions and decision rights are known. Cardinal aggregation requires stronger justification than a rank.

**Environment and boundary.** Fixed decision episode with named stakeholder population and resource envelope.

**Scope and exclusions.** Prioritization support, not automatic authorization or a claim of objectively true preferences.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Decision rights come from the relevant commitment or governance arrangement, not from an AHP weight or meeting attendance.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Compare the stored ranking computation with elicitation records and check that mandatory items were not silently scored as negotiable.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Depends on elicited alternatives and applicability; conflicts with treating every qualitative value as commensurable.

**Failure of assumptions.** An internally consistent comparison assigns low value to an obligation that the scorers cannot waive. Changing only its classification from mandatory to preference makes the computed result misleading.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Pairwise judgments grow quadratically with alternatives; tool support can alter burden. Maintenance is needed when alternatives or preferences change.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Retire the comparison when the decision is closed or its distinctions no longer affect action; reopen on material scope or stakeholder changes.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R01

**Strongest objection.** The elicitation and scoring cost can exceed its benefit and the numbers can launder disagreement.

**Known failures and misuses.** An internally consistent comparison assigns low value to an obligation that the scorers cannot waive. Changing only its classification from mandatory to preference makes the computed result misleading.

**Response or descendant form.** Retain inspectable judgments while making the scoring method conditional; compare ordinal and lightweight alternatives.

**What changed and what did not.** Numerical treatment becomes a chosen decision aid, not the definition of a valid requirement.

**Residual limits.** No universal causal claim that formal prioritization improves delivered value.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** For two obvious, reversible choices, an explained ordinal ordering and an explicit mandatory list can suffice.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-R01

**Retention status.** CONTEXT_DEPENDENT

**Retention rationale.** Retain inspectable judgments while making the scoring method conditional; compare ordinal and lightweight alternatives. No universal causal claim that formal prioritization improves delivered value.

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No sole origin, uninterrupted school or historical use of the research label Evolved Requirements Engineering is claimed. No universal reuse benefit or guarantee of complete domain modeling.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A configuration can be checked against declared feature constraints, provided feature meanings, binding stage and model version are fixed; consistency of the configuration is not sufficiency of the product for its users.

**Claim class.** MATHEMATICAL_MODEL_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** A feature-model version and a feature selection

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Individually admissible feature choices can form a prohibited combination.

**Mechanism.** Represent selection conditions, alternatives and cross-tree constraints, then evaluate their conjunction for the selected configuration.

**Mature or evolved form.** Retain formal validity within explicit domain boundaries and use targeted models where variation actually matters.

**Expected payoff.** Rejects combinations ruled out by the represented family model.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R007 supplies domain/variability framing and its limits; R008 supplies propositional analysis. R01 supplies an independent finite witness that local consistency is insufficient.

**Decision or consumer.** A configurator, product-line engineer or reviewer checking a variant.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For one product with no meaningful variants, a direct requirements review can avoid a feature model.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A family has actual optional/alternative features or cross-feature constraints.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For one product with no meaningful variants, a direct requirements review can avoid a feature model.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Feature meanings and allowed variation are stable enough to state; relevant constraints are included; optionality is not confused with universal obligation.

**Environment and boundary.** Named family, deployment mode and feature-binding stage.

**Scope and exclusions.** Logical configuration validity; physical compatibility, legal applicability and customer fitness need additional evidence.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** A valid feature choice is not necessarily permitted for every customer or jurisdiction.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Map selected options to F and evaluate phi; retain a satisfying assignment or falsified clause.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Depends on contextual applicability and versioned constraint semantics; complements, but does not replace, external validation.

**Failure of assumptions.** Selecting B without A is individually plausible but violates B implies A. R01 also shows that pairwise checks cannot establish the whole conjunction.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Domain analysis, feature interaction discovery and model maintenance; large models can exceed manual comprehensibility.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Withdraw the family model when it no longer captures intended reuse; re-enter on introduction of material variants.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R03

**Strongest objection.** The family model itself can be wrong, incomplete, too large or expensive to maintain.

**Known failures and misuses.** Selecting B without A is individually plausible but violates B implies A. R01 also shows that pairwise checks cannot establish the whole conjunction.

**Response or descendant form.** Retain formal validity within explicit domain boundaries and use targeted models where variation actually matters.

**What changed and what did not.** Formal checking strengthens an admitted configuration claim but does not turn FODA’s anticipated economics into measured benefit.

**Residual limits.** No universal reuse benefit or guarantee of complete domain modeling.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** For one product with no meaningful variants, a direct requirements review can avoid a feature model.

**Original terminology.** Domain context; reusable requirement; requirement pattern; instantiation

**Original form.** Reuse captures recurring statements and knowledge, with tailoring to a new setting.

**Original problem.** A familiar sentence keeps its wording while losing the conditions that made it appropriate.

**Locators.** §4.3: context boundaries; §5.1: feature analysis; §8.1: experience and limitations; §8.2.2.1 p.91: unmeasured reuse economics

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Reused text is a candidate until its inherited assumptions, parameter meanings, authority and configuration conditions have been re-established for the receiving context.

**Claim class.** QUALIFIED_TRANSFER_RULE

**Bearer or subject.** A requirement copied or instantiated into a new context

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A familiar sentence keeps its wording while losing the conditions that made it appropriate.

**Mechanism.** Carry provenance and applicability conditions with the reused statement, then compare the old and new contexts before accepting an inherited obligation.

**Mature or evolved form.** Use risk-directed comparison, record irreducible unknowns and prefer fresh analysis when the resemblance is weak.

**Expected payoff.** Makes context mismatches visible before they become silent constraints or omissions.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R007 exposes context and economics limits; R016 documents practice and practitioner opinions. Neither proves that a catalogue always reduces error.

**Decision or consumer.** The engineer or stakeholder accepting an inherited requirement.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a unique simple need with little useful similarity, fresh elicitation and a direct example may be cheaper than pattern infrastructure.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Text, a reference model or a pattern moves between systems, variants, customers or operating conditions.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a unique simple need with little useful similarity, fresh elicitation and a direct example may be cheaper than pattern infrastructure.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Source meaning, assumptions and authority can be recovered or explicitly marked unknown.

**Environment and boundary.** Source and destination contexts are compared at the granularity that changes obligation meaning.

**Scope and exclusions.** Reuse qualification; no assumption that a pattern becomes mandatory through popularity.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Authority must hold in the destination; the original author’s approval is not automatically transferable.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Compare parameter meanings, authority and operating assumptions; seek a case where the old and new statements imply different obligations.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Depends on traceable source context and relevant feature/configuration predicates.

**Failure of assumptions.** The identical timeout text is copied from an interactive UI into a medical control interface with a different timing envelope. Only the deployment context changes; applicability no longer follows.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Maintaining catalogues and detecting obsolete assumptions may outweigh drafting savings.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Retire a pattern when no consumer uses it or its assumptions cannot be maintained; reopen after a repeated need is demonstrated.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R04

**Strongest objection.** Most requirements have tacit context, and exhaustive context transfer is impractical.

**Known failures and misuses.** The identical timeout text is copied from an interactive UI into a medical control interface with a different timing envelope. Only the deployment context changes; applicability no longer follows.

**Response or descendant form.** Use risk-directed comparison, record irreducible unknowns and prefer fresh analysis when the resemblance is weak.

**What changed and what did not.** Reuse becomes conditional evidence-assisted instantiation, not automatic obligation inheritance.

**Residual limits.** No blanket causal error-reduction or return-on-investment claim.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** For a unique simple need with little useful similarity, fresh elicitation and a direct example may be cheaper than pattern infrastructure.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-R02

**Retention status.** RETAINED_IN_EVOLVED_FORM

**Retention rationale.** Use risk-directed comparison, record irreducible unknowns and prefer fresh analysis when the resemblance is weak. No blanket causal error-reduction or return-on-investment claim.
