## ERE-C0305 — Preserve nondominated alternatives when values are not settled

### Identity

**Property id.** ERE-C0305

**Property name.** Preserve nondominated alternatives when values are not settled

**Lineage id.** EVOLVED_REQUIREMENTS_ENGINEERING

**Property families.** ERE-FAM04; ERE-FAM13

**Record kind.** DISTINCT_CLAIM

**Parent ids.** None recorded.

**Alias or supersession ids.** None recorded.

**Discovery source ids.** ERE-S-R004; ERE-S-R015

**Native family labels.** REQUIREMENTS_ECONOMICS; CONFLICT_PRESERVATION

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** 2005 value-based agenda and 2007 multiobjective NRP

**Original terminology.** Pareto dominance; cost; stakeholder satisfaction; value proposition

**Original form.** Retain alternatives that cannot be improved in one represented objective without worsening another.

**Original problem.** A scalar score can hide disagreement or discard unsupported portions of a nonconvex tradeoff surface.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-R01

**Influence or relation class.** DOCUMENTED_ANTECEDENT

**Historical evidence and locators.** **Source id.** ERE-S-R004

**Locators.** §4.1–4.2: binary model and independent requirements; §§5–7: synthetic evaluation and discussion

**Supported part.** Native mechanism or stated limit; see source evidence capsule. The constructed cross-context rule is researcher-proposed.

**Source id.** ERE-S-R015

**Locators.** §1.2 pp.7–9: value definition and RE agenda

**Supported part.** Native mechanism or stated limit; see source evidence capsule. The constructed cross-context rule is researcher-proposed.

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No sole origin, uninterrupted school or historical use of the research label Evolved Requirements Engineering is claimed. No theorem about total welfare, fairness or complete stakeholder representation.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A nondominated set can expose unresolved tradeoffs; it does not identify a uniquely best or authorized decision, and a weighted sum can omit nondominated choices.

**Claim class.** MATHEMATICAL_AND_DECISION_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** A finite feasible alternative set with multiple declared objectives

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A scalar score can hide disagreement or discard unsupported portions of a nonconvex tradeoff surface.

**Mechanism.** Separate feasibility from objectives, retain objective direction and units, compute dominance, and preserve decision rights for choosing among surviving alternatives.

**Mature or evolved form.** Use them as deliberation aids with transparent reduction criteria, not as automatic choice rules.

**Expected payoff.** Keeps certain materially different choices visible instead of pretending the model has resolved their value conflict.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R004 defines and evaluates a multiobjective selection model. R05 is a constructed exact witness of a nondominated point missed by every positive linear weighted sum.

**Decision or consumer.** Stakeholders considering tradeoffs under an agreed feasible set.

**Alternative mechanisms.** When one feasible option dominates all others on every relevant criterion, a short dominance argument may suffice.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** Two or more outcomes conflict and no justified scalar preference resolves them.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** When one feasible option dominates all others on every relevant criterion, a short dominance argument may suffice.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Objective direction and interpretation are known; comparisons use the same context; omitted values are explicitly acknowledged.

**Environment and boundary.** Finite release alternatives; no continuous convexity assumption.

**Scope and exclusions.** Dominance in the represented objectives only, not interpersonal welfare or legitimacy.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Selecting among nondominated outcomes remains a decision by authorized parties; weights do not confer voting rights.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Compute objective vectors and pairwise dominance; check whether filtering or scalarization omitted a materially distinct option.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Feasible set must already preserve mandatory conditions; objectives depend on defensible measurement and stakeholder coverage.

**Failure of assumptions.** In R05, (2,2) needs weight w<=1/3 to beat one endpoint and w>=2/3 to beat the other. No positive linear weighting selects it although it is nondominated.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Fronts can be large and cognitively difficult to inspect; filtering must not silently remove disputed objectives.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Retire the front after the decision or rebuild it when objectives or constraints change.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R05

**Strongest objection.** Pareto sets may be too large and still encode biased objectives.

**Known failures and misuses.** In R05, (2,2) needs weight w<=1/3 to beat one endpoint and w>=2/3 to beat the other. No positive linear weighting selects it although it is nondominated.

**Response or descendant form.** Use them as deliberation aids with transparent reduction criteria, not as automatic choice rules.

**What changed and what did not.** Optimization exposes a subset of conflicts but does not reconcile values.

**Residual limits.** No theorem about total welfare, fairness or complete stakeholder representation.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** When one feasible option dominates all others on every relevant criterion, a short dominance argument may suffice.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-R01

**Retention status.** CONTEXT_DEPENDENT

**Retention rationale.** Use them as deliberation aids with transparent reduction criteria, not as automatic choice rules. No theorem about total welfare, fairness or complete stakeholder representation.

**Predicate kind.** MATHEMATICAL_MODEL_PROPERTY

**Variable domains and units.** Finite alternatives; objective coordinates retain their units and do not require summation.

**Quantifiers and scope.** All alternatives in the explicitly enumerated or correctly solved feasible set.

**Assumptions.** Objective direction and interpretation are known; comparisons use the same context; omitted values are explicitly acknowledged.

Return the alternatives not dominated within the checked feasible set. PASS for this predicate means dominance was correctly computed; no preference or authorization conclusion follows.

## ERE-C0308 — Structured assurance arguments preserve inspectability, not truth or acceptance

### Identity

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** SACM 2.3, 2023, as one version of a longer assurance-case tradition

**Original terminology.** Claim; argument; artifact evidence; assurance case; acceptance

**Original form.** An interchange metamodel represents argumentation and evidence relationships.

**Original problem.** Treating successful serialization or a complete-looking argument tree as an assurance verdict.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-R03

**Influence or relation class.** DOCUMENTED_ANTECEDENT

**Historical evidence and locators.** **Source id.** ERE-S-R014

**Locators.** §7.1–7.5 pp.11–13: scope, argumentation and evidence limitations

**Supported part.** Native mechanism or stated limit; see source evidence capsule. The constructed cross-context rule is researcher-proposed.

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No sole origin, uninterrupted school or historical use of the research label Evolved Requirements Engineering is claimed. No guarantee that the argument is complete or that accepted claims are true.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A well-formed argument model can make claims and evidence relationships inspectable while leaving their truth, relevance, inference validity and authorized acceptance unestablished.

**Claim class.** REPRESENTATION_LIMIT_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** An assurance argument and its evidence references

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Treating successful serialization or a complete-looking argument tree as an assurance verdict.

**Mechanism.** Check representation integrity separately from inference support, evidential relevance, currentness and the accepting party’s decision.

**Mature or evolved form.** Require a decision-relevant inference per retained structure and permit a simpler argument where adequate.

**Expected payoff.** Prevents a syntactic success from being silently promoted to semantic or normative success.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R014 explicitly distinguishes representation from validity and acceptance. The transfer to a commission is analytical.

**Decision or consumer.** An assurance reviewer or a consumer deciding which claim can be accepted.

**Alternative mechanisms.** A direct, bounded claim with one transparent observation may be clearer as a short statement and witness.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A structured argument is used to support a material assurance claim or transfer evidence between tools.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** A direct, bounded claim with one transparent observation may be clearer as a short statement and witness.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Claim and evidence identities are stable; evidence content can be inspected, not only linked.

**Environment and boundary.** Named subject/configuration and claim version; no implicit universal safety case.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** Additional requirement structure is justified only by a decision, failure mode or obligation it materially helps resolve; maintenance and retirement are part of that justification.

**Claim class.** QUALIFIED_ANALYST_SYNTHESIS

**Bearer or subject.** An added requirements artifact, check, model or field

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** Treating completeness of ceremony as completeness of engineering.

**Mechanism.** Name the consumer and decision, compare the expected information gain with creation/update burden, preserve necessary obligations in a simpler form where possible, and retire unused structure.

**Mature or evolved form.** Tie the cheap path to explicit retained obligations and a concrete discriminator; reopen when its conditions fail.

**Expected payoff.** Avoids paying recurring cost for structure with no demonstrated decision effect while retaining necessary constraints.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R003 demonstrates method/tool burden differences; R007 admits unmeasured economics; native artifact guidance allows contextual forms. The general decision rule is an analytical synthesis, not a measured universal law.

**Decision or consumer.** The person choosing how much structure a bounded engineering decision needs.

**Alternative mechanisms.** Use the minimal representation that makes the particular criterion, source and decision clear; one sentence and one witness can be enough.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** A proposed artifact or check adds nontrivial effort or ongoing upkeep.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** Use the minimal representation that makes the particular criterion, source and decision clear; one sentence and one witness can be enough.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** The consumer and plausible failure mode are identifiable; cheap does not mean omitting a binding or high-consequence obligation.

**Environment and boundary.** Scope, consequence, reversibility and knowledge maturity of the work.

**Scope and exclusions.** Proportionality, not permission to ignore explicitly applicable obligations.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Simplification may change representation; it cannot silently waive an obligation or approval right.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Compare what the consumer can decide using the full and minimal representations; inspect whether upkeep preserves currentness.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Depends on an accurate account of the decision and risk. Interacts with all representation-heavy properties.

**Failure of assumptions.** A reversible spelling change is forced through a large goal model and numerical priority exercise although no decision or failure mode depends on them.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Assessing proportionality itself has a cost; do not create a heavy meta-process for trivial work.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Remove structure with no live consumer, obsolete rationale or wholly redundant evidence, preserving any still-needed obligation elsewhere.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R11

**Strongest objection.** Proportionality can become an excuse for undocumented shortcuts.

**Known failures and misuses.** A reversible spelling change is forced through a large goal model and numerical priority exercise although no decision or failure mode depends on them.

**Response or descendant form.** Tie the cheap path to explicit retained obligations and a concrete discriminator; reopen when its conditions fail.

**What changed and what did not.** Maturity includes maintaining and removing structure, not merely accumulating it.

**Residual limits.** No universal optimal document size or proof that less documentation is always better.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** Use the minimal representation that makes the particular criterion, source and decision clear; one sentence and one witness can be enough.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-R02; ERE-T-R03; ERE-T-R04

**Retention status.** DUPLICATE_OR_RESTATEMENT

**Retention rationale.** Same general consumer/decision/maintenance mechanism as ERE-C0015. Retain this assigned record, its sources, decision-model examples and retirement detail; do not count a second distinct claim.

**Qualified tags.** CONTEXT_DEPENDENT; PROPORTIONALITY_EXAMPLES_RETAINED

## ERE-C0312 — Re-evaluate feature-model tests when validity semantics changes

### Identity

**Property id.** ERE-C0312

**Property name.** Re-evaluate feature-model tests when validity semantics changes

**Lineage id.** EVOLVED_REQUIREMENTS_ENGINEERING

**Property families.** ERE-FAM11; ERE-FAM15

**Record kind.** SPECIALIZATION

**Parent ids.** ERE-C0303; ERE-C0304

**Alias or supersession ids.** None recorded.

**Discovery source ids.** ERE-S-R008; ERE-S-R010

**Native family labels.** REUSE_VARIABILITY; CURRENTNESS; TEST_ORACLE_CHANGE

### Genealogy

**Historical origin.** Feature-model validity analysis and 2025-online/2026 test-evolution study

**Original terminology.** Feature-model evolution; valid configuration; test suite; mutation score; adaptation cost

**Original form.** Test generation/evolution policies respond to changed feature models.

**Original problem.** A previously passing test continues to be treated as current evidence after its oracle has changed.

**Branch ids.** ERE-BR-R02

**Influence or relation class.** DOCUMENTED_ANTECEDENT

**Historical evidence and locators.** **Source id.** ERE-S-R008

**Locators.** §§2–3: feature grammars and propositional constraints; §4: truth-maintenance propagation; References [22]: FODA

**Supported part.** Native mechanism or stated limit; see source evidence capsule. The constructed cross-context rule is researcher-proposed.

**Source id.** ERE-S-R010

**Locators.** §6.1: family/model selection; §7: construct and scalability limits; Conclusion: policy comparisons

**Supported part.** Native mechanism or stated limit; see source evidence capsule. The constructed cross-context rule is researcher-proposed.

**Disputed attribution or anachronism risk.** No sole origin, uninterrupted school or historical use of the research label Evolved Requirements Engineering is claimed. No universal best update policy or direct human-cost benefit is established.

### Claim and mechanism

**Engineering claim.** A test or expected result tied to one feature-model version must be reconsidered when changed constraints alter valid configurations; the best update policy depends on the kind of change and the cost model.

**Claim class.** SPECIALIZED_CURRENTNESS_CLAIM

**Bearer or subject.** A feature-model test, expected validity result and model version

**Failure mode or limit addressed.** A previously passing test continues to be treated as current evidence after its oracle has changed.

**Mechanism.** Bind each test oracle to the model version, classify semantic changes and evaluate regeneration versus adaptation against the current validity relation.

**Mature or evolved form.** Use change-sensitive policy choice and retain a simple regeneration path for small models.

**Expected payoff.** Avoids treating obsolete expectations as assurance of the changed family.

**Payoff evidence not just rationale.** R010 evaluates conditional policy tradeoffs; its cost metrics and scalability limits restrict the benefit claim. R06 verifies a finite stale-oracle witness.

**Decision or consumer.** The maintainer choosing which existing tests remain informative after a family change.

**Alternative mechanisms.** For a tiny model, regenerate or manually review a few configurations instead of maintaining an elaborate adaptation system.

### Applicability and authority

**Trigger or context.** The feature model or the meanings of its features change in a way that can alter configuration validity.

**Non trigger or cheap path.** For a tiny model, regenerate or manually review a few configurations instead of maintaining an elaborate adaptation system.

**Assumptions and preconditions.** Old and new constraint semantics are available; the difference is not only a text rename; test goals are explicit.

**Environment and boundary.** Versioned feature family and its test oracle, not all implementation behavior.

**Scope and exclusions.** Validity testing for feature-model evolution; mutation scores are not exhaustive detection rates for real defects.

**Authority or normative basis if applicable.** Updating the oracle to a new model does not itself authorize the new model’s obligations.

**Input and evidence provenance requirements.** Bind inputs, meanings, sources and observations to the decision/configuration version. Evaluate old and new validity on the tested configuration and inspect changed feature meanings.

**Dependencies and conflicts.** Specializes configuration validity and context-preserving reuse; also relies on trace/currentness properties in the social lane.

**Failure of assumptions.** R06 shows B without A accepted by the old unconstrained model and rejected by the new implication. Only the constraint version changed.

**Cost and maintenance burden.** Rebuilding tests, preserving meaningful coverage and estimating human update effort; syntactic edit count may misrepresent effort.

**Retirement or reentry condition.** Retire obsolete tests with reasons; re-enter old cases when a later variant restores the relevant behavior.

### Criticism and evolution

**Criticism ids.** ERE-CR-R12

**Strongest objection.** Detecting full semantic change can be costly, and measured adaptation proxies may be poor estimates of effort.

**Known failures and misuses.** R06 shows B without A accepted by the old unconstrained model and rejected by the new implication. Only the constraint version changed.

**Response or descendant form.** Use change-sensitive policy choice and retain a simple regeneration path for small models.

**What changed and what did not.** Test reuse becomes a semantic maintenance decision rather than an automatic efficiency gain.

**Residual limits.** No universal best update policy or direct human-cost benefit is established.

**Ceremony versus mechanism.** For a tiny model, regenerate or manually review a few configurations instead of maintaining an elaborate adaptation system.

**Internal tension ids.** ERE-T-R02

**Retention status.** RETAINED_IN_EVOLVED_FORM

**Retention rationale.** Use change-sensitive policy choice and retain a simple regeneration path for small models. No universal best update policy or direct human-cost benefit is established.
